paras.text: Masonry, Roofing, Siding and Exterior Finishes — Audio Lecture

This chapter covers about twenty two questions on your trade exam: nine on masonry, seven on roofing, three on siding, and a few from the finishes category. Everything here is from the twenty fifteen Michigan Residential Code and standard trade practice. The exam is closed book, so these numbers have to live in your head. Let's build them in.

Start with mortar, because it opens almost every masonry question set. There are four mortar types, and you rank them from strongest to weakest as M, S, N, O. The memory trick is the word masonwork — take every other letter and you get M, S, N, O. Type M is twenty five hundred p s i, and it goes below grade: foundations, retaining walls, anything touching earth. Type S is eighteen hundred p s i, the structural workhorse at or above grade. Type N is seven hundred fifty p s i, the general purpose mortar, and here's the thing the exam loves: Type N is the standard choice for brick veneer above grade. Don't reach for Type M just because it's strongest — strongest is not the question, application is. Type O is three hundred fifty p s i, for interior non load bearing work and repointing old soft masonry only. Grout is a different animal from mortar. Grout is fluid, at least two thousand p s i, and it gets poured into the block cells around the rebar. Mortar is stiff and goes between the units in bed and head joints, typically three eighths of an inch.

Weather rules. Cold weather masonry kicks in below forty degrees. Between twenty and forty, you heat the mixing water and sand so the mortar sits between forty and one hundred twenty degrees when you use it, and you protect finished work for twenty four hours. Below twenty degrees, no laying without a heated enclosure. And burn this in: antifreeze in mortar is never allowed. Never. Hot weather rules trigger above one hundred degrees, or above ninety with wind over eight miles an hour — shade the materials, dampen absorptive brick, fog spray the work. Mixed mortar has a board life of about two and a half hours, and you can retemper it once inside that window. One more vocabulary item: efflorescence is that white powdery salt stain on masonry. It means water is moving through the wall, dissolving salts, and leaving them behind when it evaporates. You cure the water problem — flashing and weeps — not the stain.

Now brick veneer, and this is where the numbers get dense. The air space between the veneer and the sheathing is one inch minimum, four and a half inches maximum. The veneer hangs on wall ties, and each tie can support no more than two point six seven square feet of wall. Spacing is thirty two inches on center horizontally and twenty four inches vertically. Hear the pattern: the bigger number, thirty two, runs horizontally along the course. Corrugated ties are twenty two gauge, seven eighths of an inch wide. Weep holes go in the first course, immediately above the flashing, at a maximum of thirty three inches on center, and at least three sixteenths of an inch in diameter. Here's a nasty trap pair: ties are thirty two, weeps are thirty three. Weeps get the extra inch. Lintels over veneer openings: a three by three by quarter inch steel angle spans up to six feet, with four inches of bearing at each end. And remember, veneer carries only its own weight — never floor or roof loads.

Behind every siding and veneer is the water resistive barrier — number fifteen felt or an approved housewrap — lapped two inches horizontally and six inches at vertical joints, always upper over lower, shingle fashion. That two and six pair shows up on exams.

Joints in masonry walls: clay brick expands over its life as it absorbs moisture, so brick walls get expansion joints with compressible filler. Concrete block shrinks as it cures, so block walls get control joints. Brick grows, block shrinks — opposite movements, opposite joints. Reinforcement basics: number four rebar in the grouted cells for typical residential work, and nine gauge ladder wire in the bed joints every sixteen inches, which is every other course of eight inch block.

Fireplaces and chimneys are their own cluster of numbers, and they are heavily tested. The firebox: walls are ten inches of solid masonry, or eight inches total when lined with two inches of firebrick. Firebox depth, twenty inches minimum. The hearth slab is four inches thick; the hearth extension in front is two inches thick — and it can drop to three eighths of an inch if the firebox opening is raised at least eight inches above it. The extension size depends on the opening: under six square feet, sixteen inches in front and eight inches to each side. Six square feet or bigger, twenty in front and twelve to each side. Sixteen eight, twenty twelve. Clearance to combustibles around the fireplace is two inches at the front faces and sides, and four inches at the back. The damper sits at least eight inches above the top of the opening. And the whole assembly sits on a footing at least twelve inches thick, extending six inches beyond the face on all sides, down below Michigan's forty two inch frost depth.

Chimney height is the famous three two ten rule: at least three feet above the highest point where the chimney passes through the roof, and at least two feet higher than any part of the building within ten feet horizontally. Both conditions, always. The crown on top slopes at least ten degrees, is two inches thick at the edge, and overhangs two inches. Flue sizing is a ratio of the fireplace opening: a round flue needs one twelfth of the opening area, a square or rectangular flue under a two to one shape needs one tenth, and a skinny rectangle at two to one or more needs one eighth. Quick example: a thirty six by thirty opening is one thousand eighty square inches; divided by twelve, a round flue needs ninety square inches. Chimney clearance to combustibles: two inches for a chimney inside the house or in an exterior wall, one inch for a chimney built entirely outside the walls. The split is interior versus exterior — not below versus above the roof, no matter how tempting that wrong answer looks. Last chimney item: a cricket, that little diverter roof on the uphill side, is required when the chimney is more than thirty inches wide parallel to the ridge and doesn't intersect the ridge.

Now roofing. Asphalt shingles need a slope of at least two in twelve. From two in twelve up to four in twelve, you must run double underlayment — a nineteen inch starter and thirty six inch sheets lapped nineteen inches. Four in twelve and steeper takes a single layer. Fasteners are twelve gauge roofing nails with three eighths inch heads, driven at least three quarters of an inch into the sheathing, and the code minimum is four nails per strip shingle. Six nails is a manufacturer or high wind spec, not the code floor.

Michigan cares deeply about ice. The ice barrier membrane runs from the lowest edge of the roof to at least twenty four inches inside the exterior wall line. Inside the wall line — not twenty four inches up from the eave. A big overhang means a lot more membrane. On roofs eight in twelve or steeper, it's at least thirty six inches measured along the slope. The only exemption is a detached accessory building with no conditioned space.

Drip edge extends a quarter inch below the sheathing, two inches back onto the deck, and laps two inches piece to piece. The sequencing trap: at the eaves, underlayment goes over the drip edge; at the rakes, drip edge goes over the underlayment. Step flashing where a roof meets a sidewall is four by four minimum, and at the bottom of that run you need a kickout flashing to throw water into the gutter instead of behind the siding — in Michigan that kickout is the difference between a dry wall and a rotten one. Open valley metal is twenty four inches wide.

Low slope numbers, quick and clean. Standing seam metal, a quarter in twelve. Lapped metal with sealant, half in twelve; without sealant, three in twelve. Built up roofing and single ply membranes like E P D M, a quarter in twelve. Mineral surfaced roll roofing, one in twelve. Wood shingles and wood shakes both need three in twelve on a roof, and shakes get an eighteen inch wide number thirty felt interlayment between courses. Reroofing: tear off is mandatory when the deck is water soaked, when the old roof is shake, slate, or tile, or when there are already two layers of anything up there. Two layers is the ceiling.

Attic ventilation. The base rule is one square foot of net free vent area for every one hundred fifty square feet of attic. You can cut that to one in three hundred by either of two paths: a class one or two vapor retarder on the warm side of the ceiling — but only in climate zones six, seven, and eight — or by putting forty to fifty percent of the vent area high, within three feet of the ridge, with the rest at the eaves. Either path alone is enough. And note the Michigan wrinkle: southern lower Michigan is zone five A, so down there the vapor retarder path doesn't qualify — you need the balanced vents. Keep one inch of clear air space between the insulation and the sheathing with baffles.

Siding. Fasteners generally penetrate an inch and a quarter into sheathing and framing combined. Vinyl siding lives or dies on movement: a twelve foot panel can move half an inch with temperature, so you center the nails in the slots, leave a thirty second of an inch under the head, and a quarter inch gap at the trim. Nail vinyl tight and it buckles. Installation runs bottom up: barrier, flashing, level starter strip, corners, J channel, then panels locking course over course. Fiber cement laps an inch and a quarter minimum — that's a code number — and every field cut edge gets primed. The manufacturer clearances are six inches to grade and two inches to roofing. Don't cross those wires: inch and a quarter is the lap, six inches is the grade clearance. Stucco takes three coats over lath, two coats over masonry, each coat kept moist for forty eight hours, and the weep screed at the bottom sits four inches above earth or two inches above paving.

A few finishes items round out the domain. Drywall levels: level one is tape embedded, for plenums. Level two, tape plus one coat, garages and behind tile. Level three, two coats, for heavy texture. Level four, three coats, the standard painted wall. Level five adds a skim coat over the whole surface, and it's required for gloss or semi gloss paint and critical lighting. Tile: thinset, the cement mortar, works everywhere including showers; mastic is for dry area walls only, never wet areas, never floors. Shower tile goes over cement board with a waterproof membrane — green board is not a wet area substrate. Hardwood flooring runs perpendicular to the joists, blind nailed through the tongue, with a three eighths inch expansion gap at the walls.

Rapid fire recap. Breathe, and repeat these after me. Mortar: M twenty five hundred, S eighteen hundred, N seven fifty, O three fifty — veneer gets N. Grout two thousand. Air space one inch. Ties: two point six seven square feet, thirty two horizontal, twenty four vertical, twenty two gauge. Weeps: thirty three on center, three sixteenths diameter, above the flashing. Lintel: three by three by a quarter, six foot span, four inch bearing. Felt laps: two horizontal, six vertical. Firebox: ten inches solid or eight with firebrick, twenty deep. Hearth four, extension two, or three eighths when raised eight. Extensions: sixteen and eight, or twenty and twelve at six square feet. Fireplace clearance: two front and sides, four at the back. Damper eight above the opening. Footing twelve thick, six past the face. Chimney: three feet, two feet, ten feet. Crown: ten degrees, two thick, two overhang. Flues: one twelfth round, one tenth square, one eighth skinny rectangle. Chimney clearance: two interior, one exterior. Cricket at thirty inches. Shingles: two twelve minimum, double felt below four twelve, four nails, three quarter inch penetration. Ice barrier twenty four inches inside the wall line, thirty six along the slope on steep roofs. Drip edge: quarter inch down, two onto the deck. Step flashing four by four. Valley metal twenty four. Two roof layers maximum. Vents: one fifty, or one three hundred with vapor retarder in zone six or forty to fifty percent high. Baffle space one inch. Siding nails penetrate an inch and a quarter. Fiber cement laps an inch and a quarter, six to grade. Stucco: three coats on lath, two on masonry, forty eight hour cure, screed four above earth, two above paving. Level five for gloss. Thinset in showers, never mastic.
That's the domain. Run this chapter again tomorrow, and drill the trap pairs until they can't touch you.
